questions.stem: A 46 year old woman who grew up in Bangladesh has 4 months of difficulty swallowing solids and breathlessness when climbing stairs. She had a febrile illness with joint pains as a child. She has a malar flush and an irregularly irregular pulse of 104 bpm. There is a low-pitched diastolic murmur at the apex.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Childhood rheumatic fever, malar flush, AF and an apical diastolic murmur are mitral stenosis; dysphagia comes from the enlarged left atrium compressing the oesophagus.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: febrile illness with joint pains as a child
low-pitched diastolic murmur at the apex
steps.x: Probable **rheumatic fever**, malar flush, AF and an **apical diastolic** murmur = MS. The big left atrium presses on the oesophagus.

elim: Achalasia causes dysphagia but not a murmur, malar flush or AF.
Aortic regurgitation gives an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
Oesophageal cancer causes dysphagia and weight loss but not cardiac signs.
Systemic sclerosis causes dysphagia with skin thickening and Raynaud's.

steps.x: **C. Mitral stenosis.** Rheumatic history + malar flush + apical diastolic murmur = mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has rheumatic heart disease and 1 year of increasing breathlessness on exertion. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and regular and BP 116/74 mmHg. Echocardiography later shows thickened mitral leaflets with a narrowed orifice and commissural fusion. Her GP examines her first.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation?
o: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound
Pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
Rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap at the apex
questions.e: Mitral stenosis gives a low rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex preceded by an opening snap, with a loud S1.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
A **narrowed** mitral orifice obstructs **diastolic** filling: rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with an **opening snap**.

elim: An early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge is aortic regurgitation.
An ejection systolic murmur to the carotids is aortic stenosis.
Fixed split S2 is an atrial septal defect.
A pansystolic murmur to the axilla is mitral regurgitation.

steps.x: **E. Rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap at the apex.** MS: mid-diastolic rumble + opening snap + loud S1, at the apex.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman from Ethiopia is seen at antenatal booking. She has mild breathlessness and a loud first heart sound. A medical student suspects a soft apical diastolic murmur but is unsure. The consultant asks how to examine so that the murmur is heard best.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate position for auscultation?
o: Left lateral position in full expiration with the bell at the apex
Lying flat in full inspiration at the left sternal edge
Sitting forward in full expiration at the left sternal edge
Sitting upright in full inspiration over the carotids
Standing with the diaphragm over the second right intercostal space
questions.e: The mitral stenosis murmur is low pitched and loudest at the apex with the patient rolled onto the left side in full expiration, heard with the bell.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Loud S1 + apical diastolic murmur suggests MS. Bring the apex close to the chest wall: **left lateral, expiration, bell**.

elim: Inspiration at the left sternal edge accentuates right-sided murmurs.
Sitting forward in expiration at the left sternal edge is for aortic regurgitation.
The carotids are where aortic stenosis radiates.
The second right intercostal space is the aortic area.

steps.x: **A. Left lateral position in full expiration with the bell at the apex.** MS murmur: apex, left lateral, full expiration, bell.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man in Leeds has 18 months of increasing fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance. He has no history of rheumatic fever or myocardial infarction. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and regular and BP 138/80 mmHg. The apex beat is displaced to the anterior axillary line. Echocardiography later shows a prolapsing posterior mitral leaflet.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation?
o: Ejection systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space
Mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap
Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge louder on inspiration
questions.e: Degenerative mitral valve disease is the commonest UK cause of mitral regurgitation, which gives a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, loudest on expiration.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: no history of rheumatic fever or myocardial infarction
displaced to the anterior axillary line
steps.x: A prolapsing leaflet lets blood back into the LA in **systole**: **pansystolic** murmur at the apex to the **axilla**.

elim: An ejection systolic murmur in the aortic area is aortic stenosis.
A mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap is mitral stenosis.
A pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge louder on inspiration is tricuspid regurgitation.
A friction rub is pericarditis.

steps.x: **C. Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.** MR: pansystolic, apex, radiates to the axilla.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man who injects drugs has 2 weeks of fever and rigors and now 2 days of increasing breathlessness. A pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla was not present at a clinic visit 3 months ago. He has splinter haemorrhages. His temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 112 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his mitral regurgitation?
o: Papillary muscle rupture after myocardial infarction
questions.e: A new mitral regurgitation murmur with fever and splinter haemorrhages is mitral regurgitation caused by infective endocarditis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: not present at a clinic visit 3 months ago
steps.x: **New** MR + **fever** + splinters: the valve has been damaged by **infective endocarditis**.

elim: Degenerative disease develops slowly in older people, without fever.
Dilated cardiomyopathy causes functional MR without fever or splinters.
Papillary muscle rupture follows a myocardial infarction, which he has not had.
Rheumatic disease more often causes stenosis and develops over years.

steps.x: **C. Infective endocarditis.** Fever + new MR murmur = infective endocarditis as the cause.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has 3 weeks of breathlessness and two episodes of coughing up blood-streaked sputum. She grew up in rural India. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 108/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There is a loud S1 and an opening snap. Her legs are not swollen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pregnancy increases blood volume and heart rate, unmasking rheumatic mitral stenosis, which causes dyspnoea, haemoptysis and AF; the opening snap is diagnostic.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: loud S1 and an opening snap
steps.x: Haemoptysis and AF from high left atrial pressure, plus **loud S1 + opening snap** = MS, probably rheumatic.

elim: Bronchiectasis gives chronic productive cough, not an opening snap or AF.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy gives a dilated failing LV, not an opening snap.
PE causes haemoptysis but not a loud S1 and opening snap.
TB causes haemoptysis with weight loss and sweats, not cardiac signs.

steps.x: **B. Mitral stenosis.** Loud S1 + opening snap + haemoptysis = mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man had an inferior STEMI treated with PCI 3 days ago. He suddenly becomes very breathless and sweaty. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. He has crackles throughout both lungs. There is no thrill.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation?
o: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap
Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
questions.e: Two to ten days after an inferior MI, posteromedial papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe mitral regurgitation: a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla with pulmonary oedema and shock.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: inferior STEMI treated with PCI 3 days ago
steps.x: Day 3 after an **inferior** MI with flash pulmonary oedema and shock = **papillary muscle rupture** causing acute MR.

elim: An early diastolic murmur is aortic regurgitation, not an MI complication.
A harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge, usually with a thrill, is a ventricular septal rupture.
An opening snap is chronic mitral stenosis.
A friction rub is pericarditis, which does not cause shock and pulmonary oedema.

steps.x: **D. Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.** 2 to 10 days post-MI + shock + apical pansystolic murmur = acute MR.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with known rheumatic mitral stenosis has 5 days of palpitations and worse breathlessness. She drinks no alcohol and her thyroid function is normal. Her pulse rate is 132 bpm, BP 118/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular narrow complexes with no P waves: atrial fibrillation.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of this ECG finding?
o: Left atrial dilatation from mitral stenosis
questions.e: Mitral stenosis raises left atrial pressure, dilating the atrium; chronic stretch disrupts atrial conduction and causes atrial fibrillation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
The ECG shows **AF**. The obvious cause is her **MS**, which stretches the left atrium.

elim: There is no chest pain or ST change to suggest infarction.
She drinks no alcohol.
Her thyroid function is normal.
There is nothing to suggest PE, and her saturation is normal.

steps.x: **D. Left atrial dilatation from mitral stenosis.** MS or MR: left atrial dilatation leads to AF.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with known severe mitral regurgitation wakes at 3 am gasping for breath and coughing pink frothy sputum. She cannot lie flat. Her pulse rate is 128 bpm and irregular, BP 164/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Cardiomegaly with bilateral perihilar alveolar shadowing: pulmonary oedema.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic MR with acute breathlessness, pink frothy sputum and bilateral alveolar shadowing with cardiomegaly is acute pulmonary oedema.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.
Chronic MR + sudden orthopnoea + pink frothy sputum + bat-wing shadowing = **acute pulmonary oedema**.

elim: Pneumonia gives fever and focal consolidation.
There is no COPD history, and COPD does not produce pink frothy sputum.
Massive PE causes hypotension and a clear chest X-ray.
A pneumothorax shows a visible lung edge.

steps.x: **A. Acute pulmonary oedema.** Chronic MR or MS + acute breathlessness = acute pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man had an anterior myocardial infarction 2 years ago. He has 6 months of breathlessness, fatigue and poor exercise tolerance. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and regular and BP 124/78 mmHg. The apex beat is displaced. There is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, louder in expiration. His chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A pansystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla with breathlessness and fatigue is mitral regurgitation; previous MI causing papillary muscle dysfunction is a recognised cause.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
steps.x: Apex + pansystolic + **axilla** = MR. Old MI damages the papillary muscles.

elim: Aortic stenosis is ejection systolic, radiating to the carotids.
Mitral stenosis is mid-diastolic with an opening snap.
Tricuspid regurgitation is at the left lower sternal edge and louder in inspiration.
A VSD murmur is at the left sternal edge, not radiating to the axilla.

steps.x: **B. Mitral regurgitation.** Pansystolic to the axilla = MR.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has worsening breathlessness. Echocardiography shows an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 58 mmHg. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and regular. She has a malar flush and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on auscultation?
o: Loud first heart sound and loud P2
questions.e: In mitral stenosis S1 is loud because the stiff leaflets close forcefully, and P2 is loud when pulmonary hypertension develops.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: decide what the clues add up to before reading the options.

clues: rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex
steps.x: MS gives a **loud S1**, and her **pulmonary hypertension** gives a **loud P2**.

elim: An ejection click is a bicuspid aortic valve.
S4 needs atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle; it is not an MS sign.
A quiet S1 is mitral regurgitation, or MS once leaflets are heavily calcified.
A soft S2 is severe aortic stenosis.

steps.x: **C. Loud first heart sound and loud P2.** MS: loud S1, opening snap, loud P2 if pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man develops sudden severe breathlessness and hypotension 4 days after an inferior myocardial infarction. Echocardiography shows a flail mitral leaflet with torrential mitral regurgitation from rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle.

visual.title: Culprit artery
visual.caption: The right coronary artery supplies the inferior wall and the posteromedial papillary muscle.

questions.q: Which coronary artery is most likely to have been occluded?
questions.e: The posteromedial papillary muscle usually has a single blood supply from the right coronary artery, so it ruptures after inferior MI.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.
Inferior MI is usually the **RCA**, which is the single supply to the **posteromedial** papillary muscle.

elim: The LAD supplies the anterior wall and septum.
The circumflex supplies the lateral wall and shares supply to the anterolateral muscle.
The internal mammary is a chest wall artery used for grafts.
Left main stem occlusion causes massive anterior infarction.

steps.x: **E. Right coronary artery.** Posteromedial papillary muscle: single supply from the RCA, so it ruptures after inferior MI.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation and 3 months of breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and irregular, BP 128/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. She has bibasal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
questions.e: Chronic MR overloads the left atrium and ventricle, which dilate, giving cardiomegaly; high left atrial pressure causes pulmonary oedema.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Volume overload dilates the heart (**cardiomegaly**); backpressure causes **pulmonary oedema**.

elim: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy suggests sarcoidosis.
Hyperexpansion is COPD.
Free gas under the diaphragm is a perforated viscus.
Upper zone fibrosis suggests TB or sarcoid.

steps.x: **B. Cardiomegaly with pulmonary oedema.** MR/MS CXR: cardiomegaly and pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with known mitral regurgitation has had intermittent fluttering in her chest for 2 weeks. She is breathless on hills. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: An irregularly irregular pulse in a patient with mitral valve disease suggests atrial fibrillation, which a 12-lead ECG confirms first.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Chronic MR predisposes to **AF**; confirm the rhythm with a **12-lead ECG**.

elim: Cardiac MRI is not a first test for palpitations.
Angiography looks for coronary disease.
An exercise test is for suspected angina.
TOE is invasive and used before cardioversion or for detail, not first.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG.** Irregular pulse in valve disease: 12-lead ECG for AF.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man is found to have a pansystolic murmur at the apex during a pre-operative assessment for a hernia repair. He has mild breathlessness on exertion. His pulse rate is 72 bpm, BP 130/82 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. ECG shows sinus rhythm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis and its severity?
questions.e: Transthoracic echocardiography is the gold standard for mitral valve disease, showing valve structure, the regurgitant jet and its severity.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
Any new murmur: **TTE** shows the structure and the **severity** non-invasively.

elim: Cardiac catheterisation is invasive and not needed to grade MR.
A chest X-ray shows complications, not the valve.
CT coronary angiography assesses coronary arteries.
BNP suggests heart failure but does not show the valve.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiography.** Gold standard for mitral valve disease: TTE.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman is on the coronary care unit 5 days after an inferior myocardial infarction. She suddenly becomes breathless with a new loud apical pansystolic murmur. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 90/58 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% on 4 L oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?
questions.e: Echocardiography confirms papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation, which then needs emergency mitral valve surgery.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.

clues: 5 days after an inferior myocardial infarction
steps.x: A post-MI mechanical complication is suspected: **bedside TTE** confirms it fast so she can go for **emergency surgery**.

elim: CTPA is for PE; the new murmur points to a valve problem.
Angiography shows the arteries, not the valve.
Troponin is already raised from the MI and does not show the cause.
A V/Q scan is for PE.

steps.x: **A. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography.** Post-MI new murmur + shock: bedside echo now.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with rheumatic mitral stenosis has been more breathless for a week and feels his heart racing. His pulse rate is 124 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 122/74 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. A 12-lead ECG is recorded.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the ECG?
o: Absent P waves with irregular QRS complexes
Delta waves with a short PR interval
Saw-tooth flutter waves at 300 per minute
ST elevation in V1 to V4
questions.e: Left atrial dilatation from mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation: no P waves and irregularly irregular narrow QRS complexes.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or rule out, and when.
MS + irregularly irregular pulse = **AF**: no P waves, irregular QRS.

elim: Delta waves are Wolff-Parkinson-White.
A long QT does not cause an irregularly irregular pulse.
Flutter is usually regular, with saw-tooth waves.
ST elevation in V1 to V4 is an anterior STEMI.

steps.x: **A. Absent P waves with irregular QRS complexes.** MS/MR + irregular pulse: AF on the ECG.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has moderate mitral regurgitation with a dilated left ventricle. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 38%. He is breathless on moderate exertion, in sinus rhythm and has no oedema. His BP is 134/82 mmHg and potassium 4.4 mmol/L. He is not fit for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medication to start for his LV dysfunction?
questions.e: In mitral regurgitation with LV dysfunction, ACE inhibitors such as ramipril or enalapril are used.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
MR with a **reduced ejection fraction**: start an **ACE inhibitor**.

elim: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic; he is in sinus rhythm.
Aspirin does not treat LV dysfunction.
Digoxin is used for rate control in AF or advanced failure, not first.
Verapamil is negatively inotropic and worsens LV dysfunction.

steps.x: **D. Ramipril.** MR with LV dysfunction: ACE inhibitor (ramipril, enalapril).

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has chronic moderate mitral regurgitation and newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation. Her rate is controlled on bisoprolol. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Her eGFR is 68 mL/min/1.73 m² and she has no bleeding history.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: AF in mitral valve disease needs anticoagulation to prevent stroke; her age, hypertension, diabetes and sex give a high CHA2DS2-VASc score.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
MR + AF + high stroke risk: **anticoagulate**. In MR (not moderate to severe MS) a DOAC is suitable.

elim: Aspirin does not adequately prevent AF stroke.
Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet, not an anticoagulant.
Her rate is already controlled.
Leaving her untreated exposes her to a high stroke risk.

steps.x: **A. Apixaban.** MR with AF: anticoagulation to prevent stroke.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has symptomatic rheumatic mitral stenosis and is waiting for cardiology review. She has new-onset palpitations. Her pulse rate is 128 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. She has no asthma. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medication for rate control?
questions.e: In symptomatic mitral stenosis with AF, a beta-blocker controls the rate and lengthens diastole, improving LV filling.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
AF in MS: **beta-blocker** rate control; slowing the heart gives the LV more time to fill.

elim: Adenosine is for SVT, not ongoing AF rate control.
Amlodipine does not slow the heart.
Flecainide is avoided in structural heart disease.
Ramipril is not a rate control drug.

steps.x: **C. Bisoprolol.** MS with AF: beta-blocker for rate control.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has severe degenerative mitral regurgitation from a prolapsing posterior leaflet. He is breathless on climbing one flight of stairs despite diuretics. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 58% and a dilating left ventricle. He is otherwise fit.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Increase furosemide and review in 1 year
questions.e: Severe symptomatic mitral regurgitation is treated with mitral valve repair, preferred over replacement.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Severe**, symptomatic MR in a fit patient: definitive **repair** (preferred to replacement).

elim: Balloon valvuloplasty opens a stenosed valve; it would worsen regurgitation.
Diuretics only relieve symptoms and do not fix the valve.
Waiting allows the LV to fail irreversibly.
PCI treats coronary disease, not degenerative MR.

steps.x: **D. Mitral valve repair.** Severe MR: mitral valve repair over replacement.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has severe symptomatic rheumatic mitral stenosis with a valve area of 0.8 cm². Transoesophageal echocardiography shows heavily calcified, immobile leaflets with moderate mitral regurgitation and no left atrial thrombus. She is fit for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: PBMV needs pliable leaflets without significant regurgitation; heavily calcified valves with moderate MR need open mitral valve replacement.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
Severe MS, but **calcified** and with **MR**: balloon valvuloplasty would fail or worsen MR, so **replace** the valve.

elim: Balloon valvuloplasty is for pliable, non-calcified leaflets without significant MR.
Furosemide is for symptom relief in patients unfit for surgery.
Repair is preferred for MR, not for a calcified stenotic valve.
She is severe and symptomatic, so waiting is wrong.

steps.x: **D. Mitral valve replacement.** Severe MS unsuitable for PBMV: open mitral valve replacement.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman is found to have mild rheumatic mitral stenosis on echocardiography after a murmur was heard at a sports medical. She has no symptoms, is in sinus rhythm and has no signs of heart failure. Her BP is 112/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: No medication and clinical review in 6 months
questions.e: Asymptomatic mitral stenosis without heart failure needs no medication: a watch-and-wait approach with review in 6 months and echo every 6 to 12 months.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
**Asymptomatic** and no failure: **wait and see** with follow-up.

elim: Valvuloplasty is for severe symptomatic stenosis.
Beta-blockers are for rate control in AF; she is in sinus rhythm.
Replacement is for severe disease unsuitable for valvuloplasty.
Furosemide is for fluid overload; she has none.

steps.x: **D. No medication and clinical review in 6 months.** Asymptomatic MS: no drugs, review in 6 months, echo every 6 to 12 months.

questions.stem: An 83 year old man has severe mitral regurgitation and is not fit for surgery. He has 3 weeks of increasing breathlessness and pitting oedema to the knees. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and regular, BP 142/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. He has bibasal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his symptoms?
questions.e: Diuretics such as furosemide give symptom control of fluid overload in mitral regurgitation.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
He is **fluid overloaded** and cannot have surgery: a **loop diuretic** relieves symptoms.

elim: Amlodipine causes ankle oedema and does not offload fluid.
Valvuloplasty is for stenosis, not regurgitation.
Digoxin is for rate control; he is in sinus rhythm.
Steroids cause fluid retention.

steps.x: **D. Oral furosemide.** MR fluid overload: diuretics for symptoms.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman had an inferoposterior myocardial infarction 6 days ago. She is now in cardiogenic shock. Bedside echocardiography shows a flail anterior mitral leaflet with severe mitral regurgitation from a ruptured papillary muscle. Her BP is 82/48 mmHg on inotropes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture after MI is a surgical emergency needing emergency mitral valve repair or replacement.

steps.x: A management question: decide the stage of care and what must happen now.
A **mechanical** complication with shock: only **emergency surgery** fixes it.

elim: Valvuloplasty is for stenosis.
Oral diuretics will not reverse cardiogenic shock from a flail leaflet.
Thrombolysis does not repair a ruptured muscle.
ACE inhibitors drop BP further in shock.

steps.x: **B. Emergency mitral valve surgery.** Papillary muscle rupture: emergency mitral valve repair or replacement.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman has rheumatic mitral stenosis with a valve area of 1.0 cm². She has had several episodes of coughing up small amounts of bright red blood. Chest X-ray shows an enlarged left atrium and upper lobe venous diversion. She has no fever or weight loss.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her haemoptysis?
o: Erosion of a bronchial artery by tumour
Infarction of the lung from emboli
Raised left atrial pressure transmitted to the pulmonary veins
questions.e: The narrowed valve obstructs LV filling, raising left atrial pressure, which backs up into the pulmonary veins; dilated bronchial veins rupture causing haemoptysis.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.

clues: enlarged left atrium and upper lobe venous diversion
steps.x: Obstructed filling raises **LA pressure**, which is passed back into the **pulmonary veins**.

elim: Bronchiectasis causes haemoptysis with chronic sputum.
Tumours cause haemoptysis with weight loss; she has none.
Pulmonary infarction is from PE, not the mechanism here.
Nothing suggests thrombocytopenia.

steps.x: **E. Raised left atrial pressure transmitted to the pulmonary veins.** MS haemoptysis: high LA pressure backs into the pulmonary circulation.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has had severe mitral regurgitation for several years. Echocardiography now shows a dilated left atrium of 58 mm, a dilated left ventricle and an ejection fraction of 40%. He has recently developed atrial fibrillation and ankle oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of these changes?
o: Pressure overload of the left ventricle
Volume overload of the left atrium and ventricle
questions.e: Blood flowing back into the left atrium in systole volume-overloads the LA and LV; LA dilatation causes AF and LV dilatation leads to heart failure.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.
Regurgitant blood returns every beat: **volume overload**. LA dilates (AF), LV dilates and fails.

elim: Coronary stenosis causes ischaemia, not this valve pattern.
Pressure overload is aortic stenosis or hypertension and causes LV hypertrophy.
Infiltration is amyloid or sarcoid, with a non-dilated ventricle.
RV outflow obstruction is pulmonary stenosis.

steps.x: **E. Volume overload of the left atrium and ventricle.** MR = volume overload: LA dilatation (AF) and LV dilatation (heart failure).

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman who grew up in Pakistan had a sore throat followed by painful migrating joints at age 10. She now has mitral stenosis. Transthoracic echocardiography is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely appearance of the mitral valve?
o: Normal leaflets with a dilated annulus
Ruptured chordae with a flail leaflet
questions.e: Rheumatic fever triggers autoimmune damage by molecular mimicry, causing fibrosis, calcification and commissural fusion that narrows the orifice.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding in the stem to the mechanism behind it.

clues: sore throat followed by painful migrating joints
steps.x: Rheumatic damage scars the leaflets: **thickening**, calcification and **commissural fusion**.

elim: A bicuspid valve with a raphe is a congenital aortic valve.
Floppy leaflets are degenerative prolapse causing regurgitation.
A dilated annulus causes functional regurgitation, not stenosis.
Ruptured chordae cause acute regurgitation.
